title: Vows of Chan Master Yishan Huiran

source.text: Chan Master Yishan Huiran, Vows (included in Admonitions for the Monastic Gate and other collections)
source.translationLicense: English translation and commentary: newly made by Sutra Box from its own Korean version (based on an AI draft, still being reviewed and refined)

h01.heading: Refuge in the Three Jewels
h01.plain: I bow my head to the Buddhas of the ten directions, to the pure and wondrous teaching, and to the liberated holy Sangha. Out of compassion, have pity on me and take me in.
h01.commentary: "The tamer" is the teacher who skillfully tames beings: the Buddha. The aspiration begins by taking refuge in the Buddha, Dharma and Sangha.

h02.heading: Repentance
h02.plain: I turned my back on my true nature and wrongly entered the stream of delusion, drifting with birth and death, chasing sights and sounds, craving and stained by them. I piled up the leaking karma of affliction and with the six senses committed endless wrongs, sinking into the sea of suffering and deep into wrong paths. I put myself forward and coveted what was others', raising the crooked to press down the straight. For the karmic obstacles and all the faults of many lives, I look up to the compassion of the Three Jewels and repent with my whole heart.
h02.commentary: In the original, "so-and-so" marks the place where chanters say their own name.

h03.heading: Please Save Me
h03.plain: May the Buddha save me and good friends guide me, so that I leave the deep source of affliction and reach the far shore of awakening. May my blessings and life in this world flourish, and in lives to come may the seeds of wisdom and the spiritual sprouts grow well together.
h03.commentary: "The Capable and Kind" translates the name Śākyamuni. Good friends are those who help one's practice: spiritual friends.

h04.heading: Leaving Home and Pure Practice
h04.plain: May I be born where the Buddha-Dharma is, meet a wise teacher, leave home young with right faith, and enter the Way. May my six senses be clear, my body, speech and mind gentle and even, untainted by worldly ties, always cultivating pure conduct. May I keep the precepts firmly so that not a speck of karma intrudes, and keep my bearing dignified so that I harm not even a small flying insect. May I meet none of the eight difficulties, lack none of the four supports of practice, let the wisdom of prajñā shine forth, and never turn back from the mind of awakening.
h04.commentary: "The central land" here is not a country's name but "the land where the Buddha-Dharma is." The eight difficulties are eight situations in which it is hard to meet the Dharma; the four supports are the four things practice needs.

h05.heading: The Bodhisattva Path
h05.plain: May I practice the true Dharma and awaken to the Great Vehicle, open the gate of the six pāramitās, and cross the ocean of asaṃkhyeya kalpas. May I raise the banner of the Dharma everywhere, tear through the many-layered net of doubt, subdue every Māra, and carry on and revive the Three Jewels. May I serve the Buddhas of the ten directions tirelessly, learn and master every Dharma gate, make merit and wisdom widely to benefit beings as countless as dust, gain the six spiritual powers, and attain Buddhahood in a single life.
h05.commentary: The six pāramitās are giving, precepts, patience, diligence, meditation and wisdom. The three asaṃkhyeya kalpas are the time a bodhisattva practices until becoming a Buddha.

h06.heading: Into the World of Beings
h06.plain: Even then, may I not leave the Dharma realm but enter everywhere into the world full of affliction, practicing Avalokiteśvara's compassionate heart and Samantabhadra's ocean of vows. In other worlds and in this one, may I take forms suited to every kind of being and spread the wondrous Dharma; in the paths of hells and hungry ghosts, may I send forth great light or show spiritual powers, so that all who see my form or merely hear my name arouse the mind of awakening and forever leave the suffering of saṃsāra.
h06.commentary: This is the bodhisattva's vow not to rest alone after awakening but to go back among beings. The original word for hell here is nīraya.

h07.heading: Turning Suffering into Joy
h07.plain: May the hells of boiling cauldrons and icy rivers turn into fragrant groves, and those who drink molten copper and eat iron be reborn in the Pure Land. May the bitterness of creatures who wear fur and bear horns, and of those bound by debt and resentment, all come to an end, and may they all share in benefit and joy. In times of plague, may I become medicinal herbs to heal long illness; in times of famine, may I become grain to save the poor and hungry; and may I bring about whatever is of benefit.
h07.commentary: "Wearing fur and bearing horns" means animals. The lines about becoming herbs and grain are especially loved in this aspiration.

h08.heading: Dedication
h08.plain: And may the enemies and friends of many lives and my present family be freed from floundering in the four kinds of birth, let go of the attachments of ten thousand kalpas, and attain the Buddha way together with all living things. Space may come to an end, but my vows are endless; may the sentient and the insentient alike attain complete wisdom.
h08.commentary: "Space may end, but my vows are endless" is the most quoted closing line of this aspiration.
